candidates.text: He had walked that stretch of cliff a thousand times in twenty-two years of nights, and he knew every seam and shelf of the wet stone — so he knew the door had no business being there. It was set flush into the rock, oak and iron, the kind of door that belonged to a churchyard or a sea captain's hold, and it was not damp, not weathered, not marked by spray. The brass handle shone as though someone had polished it that morning. He tried the light from his lantern across the panels and found no hinges, no frame, no gap where a frame might hide; the door simply *was*, the way a word is simply in a sentence. Behind it, when he pressed his ear to the wood, he heard something that took him a long moment to identify, because it was so ordinary that it made no sense at all: a woman humming, and the clink of a kettle, and further off, the sound of a clock striking noon in a room with no windows. He should have turned around then. He should have gone up the stairs and written it in the log and let the district office send men with lamps and sensible questions. Instead, he found himself reaching for the latch, thinking, absurdly, of the milk he had left on the gallery rail that morning — of how it would be spoiled by now, of how disappointed the mainlanders would be — and thinking too of his wife, who had died in the winter of the fever and had never once, in all the years since, knocked on a door before entering. The latch was cold. It turned. The humming stopped.

He had walked that stretch of cliff a hundred times, and he knew it in his bones — the seam of iron pyrite that glittered near the north corner, the ledge where the gulls nested, the patch of turf that stayed green all winter. So he was not mistaken when the path brought him to the place where the rock should have been solid: a narrow iron door, set flush into the cliff, its hinges crusted with rust a century deep, its frame warped so the sea air had got into it and left a long white bloom of salt. He stood a long while before touching it, because what troubled him was not the door but the shape it made in his certainty. Yesterday the cliff had been unbroken. He had laid his own hand on that exact square of stone to steady himself while a storm came in, and it had been cold and seamless and given under his palm the way stone gives. He set down the lantern and lifted the latch. It turned. Behind the door, stairs went down into a darkness that smelled of dry paper and lamp oil, and somewhere far below, faint as a heartbeat through the rock, something was keeping a light.

He had walked that stretch of cliff every evening for eleven years—lamp trimmed, wick turned up, the beam swinging out over black water—and he knew every seam and ledge of the granite the way he knew the ticks of the clock in the lamp room. So the door could not have been there. It sat low in the rock where the cliff's face was laced with quartz: a slab of black oak banded with iron, its hinges furred with rust that crumbled orange under his thumb, and the brass handle, when he turned it, gave warm and smooth as a knob polished a thousand times. The door swung inward without a creak, breathing out a smell of beeswax and hot oil and something sweeter beneath, honey perhaps, or the ghost of a pipe smoked a long while ago. Within, steps descended in a slow spiral, cut square and true, and far below the last of the light something moved with the patient rhythm of tide working a cavern, or of breath. Above him the beam swept the sea and found nothing. He stood a long while with one hand on the frame, listening, and then, because he was a keeper and the dark was his business, he went down.

instruction: Answer the brief as you normally would.

task.brief: A lighthouse keeper finds a door in the cliff below the lamp room that was not there yesterday. Write the next paragraph.
good_idea_qualities: the door implies a consequence the keeper must act on
the paragraph keeps the sea and the lamp in view
something is at stake for the keeper personally
task.reference_text: The keeper set the oil can down and counted the door twice, the way he counted ships. It was blue, salt-blistered, and hinged on the seaward side, which meant whoever built it had worked from the water.
